differences.title: 1. DATA MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Neo4j stores nodes/relationships plus properties in a property-graph model with identity-based entities. Cypher patterns compile into index seeks and traversals, driven by relationship direction, labels, and property predicates.
differences.rightDesc: Amazon Neptune supports the openCypher-compatible property graph model. It organizes graph structures internally for efficient pattern matching and traversals, with indexes and statistics guiding query planning for label/property constraints.

differences.title: 2. QUERY PIPELINE
differences.leftDesc: Neo4j’s Cypher compiler rewrites declarative queries into a logical plan, applies rule-based optimizations, then executes using operator pipelines (expand, filter, hash/merge). Cost-based decisions rely on cardinality estimates.
differences.rightDesc: Neptune translates openCypher or Gremlin traversals into an internal execution representation. It performs planning optimizations and uses traversal-oriented operators, balancing eager vs pipelined steps for patterns.

differences.title: 3. STORAGE & INDEXING
differences.leftDesc: Neo4j (when using its native storage) relies on a transactional graph store with indexes for labels and properties, plus relationship-structuring optimized for neighborhood traversals. Writes update indexes and transaction logs.
differences.rightDesc: Neptune is a managed service using distributed persistence optimized for graph access. It maintains support structures for fast neighbor lookups and indexes for labels/properties, while abstracting hardware layout.

differences.title: 4. TRANSACTIONS & CONSISTENCY
differences.leftDesc: Neo4j provides strong transactional semantics for graph updates. It uses journaling/transaction logs to ensure atomic writes and crash recovery, coordinating commits with lock management for concurrent traversals.
differences.rightDesc: Neptune provides transactional behavior suitable for online graph workloads, with service-managed durability and recovery. It coordinates concurrent reads and writes through internal concurrency control and replicated persistence mechanisms.

differences.title: 5. SCALING STRATEGY
differences.leftDesc: Neo4j commonly scales by clustering/replication patterns (e.g., causal clustering) and by tuning memory/IO for traversal locality. Write throughput can be a constraint due to leader-based coordination.
differences.rightDesc: Neptune scales through AWS-managed capacity, using reader endpoints/replicas for read-heavy traffic and multi-AZ deployment for resilience. It limits some bottlenecks by offloading read workload from the writer.

differences.title: 6. OPERATIONS & OBSERVABILITY
differences.leftDesc: With Neo4j, engineers manage lifecycle: deployment, tuning heap/page cache, configuring clustering, and operating backups/restore. Observability comes from server metrics plus query profiling tools like EXPLAIN/PROFILE.
differences.rightDesc: Neptune shifts operational burden to AWS: patching, scaling primitives, and managed backups. You typically use CloudWatch metrics and Neptune-specific query/execution diagnostics, plus tracing/logging hooks for performance triage.

differences.title: 7. ECOSYSTEM & INTEGRATIONS
differences.leftDesc: Neo4j’s ecosystem is rich around Cypher tooling, drivers, and graph analytics integrations. Developers can leverage mature libraries for ETL, graph algorithms, and embedding into application stacks with stable versions.
differences.rightDesc: Neptune integrates tightly with AWS services for IAM, networking, and data pipelines. It aligns with AWS deployment models and supports common graph-access patterns from within the cloud, simplifying secure connectivity.
